query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractRefractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are of interest for ultrahigh-temperature applications. To overcome their drawbacks — low-temperature brittleness and poor creep strength at high temperatures — improved fundamental understanding is needed. Using experiments, theory, and modeling, we investigated prototypical body-centered cubic (BCC) RHEAs, TiZrHfNbTa and VNbMoTaW. The former is compressible to 77 K, whereas the latter is not below 298 K. Hexagonal close-packed (HCP) elements in TiZrHfNbTa lower its dislocation core energy, increase lattice distortion, and lower its shear modulus relative to VNbMoTaW whose elements are all BCC. Screw dislocations dominate TiZrHfNbTa plasticity, but equal numbers of edges and screws exist in VNbTaMoW. Dislocation cores are compact in VNbTaMoW and extended in TiZrHfNbTa, and different macroscopic slip planes are activated in the two RHEAs, which we attribute to the concentration of HCP elements. However, a single-phase RHEA, TiZrHfNbTa, was recently shown to be significantly weaker in creep than CMSX-4 despite the former’s higher melting point. The weakness was ascribed to two factors: faster diffusion in the BCC matrix of the RHEA relative to the FCC matrix of CMSX-4 and a lack of precipitates. Additional research is therefore needed to enhance the creep strength of TiZrHfNbTa, for example, by the introduction of suitable strengthening precipitates. Meanwhile, RHEAs with higher melting points must also be investigated since diffusion will be slower in such materials. One such RHEA is VNbMoTaW, whose melting point is ~500 °C higher than TiZrHfNbTa,,. However, it has a major disadvantage: lack of ductility at room temperature even in compression. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. decision.trend: Research has been focused on improving the room-temperature ductility of refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) without compromising their high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance. Earlier studies have explored various strategies, including microstructural engineering, thermomechanical treatments, and composition optimization. A common theme is the importance of controlling the microstructure and dislocation behavior to achieve improved ductility.
decision.unsolved: Despite progress, the poor room-temperature ductility of RHEAs remains a significant challenge. The underlying mechanisms governing ductility and strength in these alloys are not yet fully understood, and further research is needed to develop effective strategies for improving their mechanical properties.
decision.why: The introduction of HCP elements, such as Ti or Zr, into BCC RHEAs has been shown to enhance ductility by reducing dislocation core energy, increasing lattice distortion, and lowering the shear modulus. This approach has been demonstrated to be effective in improving the mechanical properties of RHEAs, and further research is warranted to explore its potential for improving the room-temperature ductility of Equal-atomic NbMoTaW.
